html:
The Sound Dues were a toll that Denmark charged every ship passing through the Øresund, the strait between Denmark and Sweden, from 1429 to 1857.

King Eric of Pomerania began them. Ships had to stop at Helsingør, under the guns of the castle later rebuilt as Kronborg, the Elsinore of Shakespeare's Hamlet. Since Baltic grain, timber and iron went west through the Sound, the toll made the Danish crown rich and independent of its nobles. Its records are a main source for the trade of early modern Europe.

Control of the Sound drew Sweden, the Dutch and England into Denmark's wars, and the loss of its eastern shore in the Treaty of Roskilde weakened it. The United States refused to pay, and in 1857 the maritime powers bought the toll out. Today the Øresund Bridge crosses the strait. See also the Hanseatic League.
